q: What does AWS EFS stand for?

exp.a: Correct. EFS stands for Elastic File System, a fully managed file storage service.
exp.b: Incorrect. The correct expansion is Elastic File System, not Storage.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS stands for Elastic File System, not Encrypted File System.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS stands for Elastic File System, not Extended File Service.

q: What type of file system protocol does Amazon EFS use?

exp.a: Incorrect. SMB is used by Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, not EFS.
exp.b: Correct. Amazon EFS uses NFSv4.0 and NFSv4.1 protocol.
exp.c: Incorrect. FTP is a file transfer protocol, not used by EFS.
exp.d: Incorrect. iSCSI is a block-level protocol used with storage solutions, not EFS.

q: Amazon EFS is compatible with which operating system?

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS is not compatible with Windows. Use FSx for Windows File Server instead.
exp.b: Correct. Amazon EFS is compatible with Linux-based AMIs only.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS supports only Linux-based instances.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS is designed for Linux-based EC2 instances.

q: How many Availability Zones can Amazon EFS store data across within a region?

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS stores data across multiple AZs for high availability (EFS One Zone stores in 1 AZ).
exp.b: Incorrect. Standard EFS stores data across 3 or more AZs in a region.
exp.c: Correct. EFS Standard storage class stores data redundantly across multiple (3+) AZs.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS is a regional service that spans multiple AZs.

q: What is the maximum storage capacity of Amazon EFS?

opts.c: No pre-provisioned limit – scales to petabytes automatically

exp.a: Incorrect. 16 TB is the max size of a single EBS volume, not EFS.
exp.b: Incorrect. EFS has no fixed storage limit of 64 TB.
exp.c: Correct. EFS automatically scales up to petabytes without pre-provisioning.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS can scale to petabytes but it grows and shrinks automatically.

q: How many EC2 instances can concurrently connect to a single Amazon EFS file system?

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS is designed for shared access across many instances.
exp.b: Incorrect. EFS supports far more than 10 instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS can handle more than 100 concurrent connections.
exp.d: Correct. EFS supports thousands of concurrent EC2 instance connections.

q: Which of the following is a storage class available in Amazon EFS?

exp.a: Correct. EFS Standard is one of the storage classes (others include EFS Standard-IA, EFS One Zone, EFS One Zone-IA).
exp.b: Incorrect. Glacier is an S3 storage class, not an EFS storage class.
exp.c: Incorrect. Deep Archive is an S3 storage class, not EFS.
exp.d: Incorrect. Provisioned is not a storage class; Provisioned Throughput is a throughput mode.

q: What does EFS Infrequent Access (IA) storage class provide?

opts.a: Higher performance for frequently accessed data
opts.b: Lower cost for data that is not accessed every day

exp.a: Incorrect. IA is for infrequently accessed data, not high-performance frequent access.
exp.b: Correct. EFS IA provides lower storage cost for files not accessed every day.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS IA is not archival; files are accessible immediately without retrieval delays.
exp.d: Incorrect. IA is a cost-optimization class, not an encryption-specific class.

q: What is the cost savings percentage when using EFS Infrequent Access compared to EFS Standard?

exp.a: Incorrect. The savings are much higher than 50%.
exp.b: Incorrect. The savings can be higher than 72%.
exp.c: Correct. EFS IA can provide up to 92% lower cost compared to EFS Standard.
exp.d: Incorrect. The savings are significantly more than 30%.

q: Which feature automatically moves files between EFS storage classes based on access patterns?

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS Replication copies data to another region, not between storage classes.
exp.b: Correct. EFS Lifecycle Management automatically moves files to IA based on access patterns.
exp.c: Incorrect. Bursting is a throughput mode, not a data movement feature.
exp.d: Incorrect. Provisioned Throughput is for setting specific throughput levels.

q: After how many days of not being accessed can a file be moved to EFS IA using Lifecycle Management?

exp.a: Correct. EFS Lifecycle policies can be set to 7, 14, 30, 60, or 90 days.
exp.b: Incorrect. Multiple lifecycle policy durations are available.
exp.c: Incorrect. 1 day is not a valid lifecycle policy duration for EFS.
exp.d: Incorrect. There are more options than just 60 or 90 days.

q: What are the two throughput modes available in Amazon EFS?

exp.a: Incorrect. Standard and Enhanced are not EFS throughput modes.
exp.b: Correct. EFS offers Bursting Throughput and Provisioned Throughput modes (also Elastic throughput).
exp.c: Incorrect. On-Demand and Reserved are EC2 pricing models.
exp.d: Incorrect. General Purpose and Max I/O are performance modes, not throughput modes.

q: What are the two performance modes available in Amazon EFS?

exp.a: Incorrect. Bursting and Provisioned are throughput modes.
exp.b: Incorrect. These are not valid EFS performance modes.
exp.c: Correct. EFS has General Purpose (default) and Max I/O performance modes.
exp.d: Incorrect. These are not the official names of EFS performance modes.

q: Which EFS performance mode is recommended for most workloads?

exp.a: Incorrect. Max I/O is for highly parallelized workloads requiring higher throughput.
exp.b: Correct. General Purpose is the default and recommended for latency-sensitive use cases like web serving and CMS.
exp.c: Incorrect. Provisioned is a throughput mode, not a performance mode.
exp.d: Incorrect. Bursting is a throughput mode, not a performance mode.

q: What is the maximum throughput per file system in EFS Bursting Throughput mode for Standard storage?

exp.a: Correct. In Bursting mode, throughput scales at 50 MiB/s per TiB baseline and bursts to 100 MiB/s per TiB.
exp.b: Incorrect. 50 MiB/s per TiB is the baseline, but burst can reach 100 MiB/s per TiB.
exp.c: Incorrect. 250 MiB/s is not the burst rate per TiB.
exp.d: Incorrect. 1 GiB/s per TiB is not the correct burst throughput.

q: What is the default baseline throughput in EFS Bursting mode per TiB of Standard storage?

exp.a: Incorrect. 100 MiB/s is the burst throughput, not the baseline.
exp.b: Correct. The baseline throughput in Bursting mode is 50 MiB/s per TiB of storage.
exp.c: Incorrect. 25 MiB/s is not the correct baseline.
exp.d: Incorrect. 150 MiB/s is not the correct baseline throughput.

q: What encryption does Amazon EFS support?

opts.c: Both encryption at rest and in transit

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS supports both at rest and in transit encryption.
exp.b: Incorrect. EFS supports both at rest and in transit encryption.
exp.c: Correct. EFS supports encryption at rest using KMS and encryption in transit using TLS.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS fully supports encryption.

q: Which AWS service is used to manage encryption keys for EFS encryption at rest?

exp.a: Incorrect. CloudHSM provides hardware security modules but EFS uses KMS by default.
exp.b: Correct. EFS uses AWS KMS to manage encryption keys for encryption at rest.
exp.c: Incorrect. Secrets Manager is for storing secrets, not for EFS encryption keys.
exp.d: Incorrect. Certificate Manager manages SSL/TLS certificates, not EFS encryption keys.

q: What is a Mount Target in Amazon EFS?

opts.a: A backup copy of the file system
opts.b: An endpoint in an Availability Zone that EC2 instances use to mount the file system
opts.c: A snapshot of the file system
opts.d: A replication of the file system to another region

exp.a: Incorrect. A mount target is not a backup.
exp.b: Correct. A mount target is a network endpoint in a VPC subnet/AZ through which instances access EFS.
exp.c: Incorrect. Mount targets are not snapshots.
exp.d: Incorrect. Mount targets are not cross-region replications.

q: How many mount targets can you create per Availability Zone for an EFS file system?

exp.a: Incorrect. There is a limit of one mount target per AZ.
exp.b: Correct. You can create one mount target per Availability Zone for a standard EFS file system.
exp.c: Incorrect. Only 1 mount target per AZ is allowed.
exp.d: Incorrect. Only 1 mount target per AZ is allowed.

q: Which of the following services CANNOT directly use Amazon EFS?

exp.a: Incorrect. EC2 instances can mount EFS file systems.
exp.b: Incorrect. Lambda functions can mount EFS file systems.
exp.c: Correct. S3 is an object storage service and does not mount EFS. They are separate services.
exp.d: Incorrect. ECS with Fargate can mount EFS file systems.

q: Can AWS Lambda functions use Amazon EFS?

opts.b: Yes, Lambda can mount EFS file systems

exp.a: Incorrect. Lambda supports EFS as well.
exp.b: Correct. AWS Lambda functions can mount EFS file systems for persistent, shared storage.
exp.c: Incorrect. No special add-on is needed; it is natively supported.
exp.d: Incorrect. Lambda can both read and write to EFS.

q: Amazon EFS is a _____ storage service.

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS is block storage, not EFS.
exp.b: Incorrect. S3 is object storage, not EFS.
exp.c: Correct. Amazon EFS is a managed file storage service.
exp.d: Incorrect. Glacier is archive storage, not EFS.

q: Which of the following is TRUE about Amazon EFS?

opts.a: It can only be mounted by one EC2 instance at a time
opts.b: It is a regional service that can be accessed across multiple AZs
opts.d: It only works with Windows instances

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS supports concurrent access from thousands of instances.
exp.b: Correct. EFS is a regional service accessible from multiple AZs within a region.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS automatically scales storage capacity.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS works only with Linux-based instances.

q: What is the EFS One Zone storage class?

opts.a: Data is stored in multiple AZs for high availability
opts.b: Data is stored in a single Availability Zone to reduce cost
opts.c: Data is stored in multiple regions
opts.d: Data is encrypted with a one-time key

exp.a: Incorrect. That describes EFS Standard, not One Zone.
exp.b: Correct. EFS One Zone stores data in a single AZ, offering lower cost with reduced availability.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS One Zone is within a single AZ, not multiple regions.
exp.d: Incorrect. One Zone refers to the AZ placement, not encryption.

q: How much cost savings does EFS One Zone provide compared to EFS Standard?

exp.a: Incorrect. The savings are higher than 25%.
exp.b: Correct. EFS One Zone provides up to 47% savings compared to EFS Standard.
exp.c: Incorrect. 75% is not the correct savings figure.
exp.d: Incorrect. 90% is not the correct savings for One Zone vs Standard.

q: What is the availability SLA for EFS Standard storage class?

exp.a: Incorrect. 99.9% is not the SLA for EFS Standard.
exp.b: Correct. EFS Standard offers 99.99% availability.
exp.c: Incorrect. 99.999% is not the advertised SLA.
exp.d: Incorrect. 99.95% is not the EFS Standard SLA.

q: What is the availability SLA for EFS One Zone storage class?

exp.a: Incorrect. 99.99% is for EFS Standard.
exp.b: Correct. EFS One Zone offers 99.9% availability (lower than Standard due to single AZ).
exp.c: Incorrect. 99.95% is not the One Zone SLA.
exp.d: Incorrect. 99.5% is not the correct SLA.

q: Which port must be open in the security group for EC2 instances to mount an EFS file system?

exp.a: Incorrect. Port 80 is for HTTP traffic, not NFS.
exp.b: Incorrect. Port 443 is for HTTPS, not NFS.
exp.c: Correct. Port 2049 must be open for NFS traffic to mount EFS.
exp.d: Incorrect. Port 22 is for SSH access, not for mounting EFS.

q: Which of the following can be used to control access to Amazon EFS?

exp.a: Correct. EFS access can be controlled using security groups, IAM policies, and EFS access points.
exp.b: Incorrect. Security groups are also used for EFS mount target access control.
exp.c: Incorrect. IAM policies and access points are also used.
exp.d: Incorrect. NACLs can control network traffic but are not the primary EFS access control.

q: What is an EFS Access Point?

opts.b: An application-specific entry point to an EFS file system that enforces a user identity and directory

exp.a: Incorrect. Access points are not VPN connections.
exp.b: Correct. EFS Access Points provide application-specific entry points enforcing user identity, permissions, and root directory.
exp.c: Incorrect. Access points are not backup recovery points.
exp.d: Incorrect. Access points are not cross-region endpoints.

q: Does Amazon EFS support automatic backups?

opts.a: No, you must manually create backups
opts.d: No, EFS does not support any backup

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS supports automatic backups through AWS Backup.
exp.b: Correct. EFS integrates with AWS Backup for automatic and scheduled backups.
exp.c: Incorrect. Backups are managed by AWS Backup, not directly to S3.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS fully supports backup via AWS Backup.

q: Can Amazon EFS be accessed from on-premises servers?

opts.b: Yes, via AWS Direct Connect or VPN
opts.c: Yes, but only using S3 gateway
opts.d: No, it requires a dedicated physical connection only

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS can be accessed from on-premises.
exp.b: Correct. On-premises servers can access EFS via AWS Direct Connect or AWS VPN.
exp.c: Incorrect. S3 gateway is for S3, not EFS.
exp.d: Incorrect. Both Direct Connect and VPN work; a dedicated connection is not mandatory.

q: What is the pricing model for Amazon EFS?

opts.b: Pay only for the storage you use (no pre-provisioning)
opts.c: Flat monthly fee regardless of usage
opts.d: Pay per number of files stored

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS charges for actual storage used, not pre-provisioned capacity.
exp.b: Correct. EFS uses a pay-as-you-go model; you pay only for storage used.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS does not have a flat monthly fee.
exp.d: Incorrect. Pricing is based on GB stored, not number of files.

q: What is the approximate cost of EFS Standard storage per GB per month (US East region)?

exp.a: Correct. EFS Standard storage costs approximately $0.30 per GB per month.
exp.b: Incorrect. $0.08 is closer to EBS pricing, not EFS Standard.
exp.c: Incorrect. $0.023 is the cost of S3 Standard storage, not EFS.
exp.d: Incorrect. $0.50 is too high for EFS Standard.

q: What is the approximate cost of EFS Infrequent Access storage per GB per month?

exp.a: Incorrect. $0.30 is the EFS Standard price.
exp.b: Correct. EFS IA costs approximately $0.025/GB/month for storage plus per-access charges.
exp.c: Incorrect. $0.10 is not the correct IA pricing.
exp.d: Incorrect. $0.005 is too low; that's closer to Glacier pricing.

q: How does EFS compare to EBS in terms of multi-instance access?

opts.b: EFS supports multi-instance access; EBS is typically single-instance
opts.c: EBS supports multi-instance access; EFS is single-instance

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS multi-attach is limited to io1/io2 volumes and specific use cases.
exp.b: Correct. EFS natively supports thousands of concurrent connections; EBS is typically attached to one instance (with limited multi-attach for io1/io2).
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS is the shared file system, not EBS.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS supports multi-instance access.

q: What is the difference between EFS and Amazon S3?

opts.a: EFS is file storage with hierarchy; S3 is object storage with flat namespace
opts.b: EFS is object storage; S3 is file storage
opts.d: EFS is block storage; S3 is file storage

exp.a: Correct. EFS is a file system (hierarchical), while S3 is object storage (flat structure with key-value).
exp.b: Incorrect. It's the other way around.
exp.c: Incorrect. They serve different purposes.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS is file storage, and EBS is block storage.

q: Which AWS service provides a Windows-compatible shared file system?

opts.b: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS only supports Linux (NFS protocol).
exp.b: Correct. FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB-based shared file storage for Windows.
exp.c: Incorrect. S3 is object storage, not a shared file system.
exp.d: Incorrect. EBS is block storage attached to individual instances.

q: What is the maximum file size supported in Amazon EFS?

exp.a: Incorrect. 5 TB is the max object size in S3.
exp.b: Correct. The maximum individual file size in EFS is 47.9 TiB.
exp.c: Incorrect. 16 TB is the max EBS volume size.
exp.d: Incorrect. 52.2 TiB is not the correct maximum file size.

q: What is the maximum number of file systems you can create per AWS account per region (default)?

exp.a: Incorrect. The default limit is higher than 10.
exp.b: Incorrect. The default limit is higher than 100.
exp.c: Correct. The default limit is 1,000 EFS file systems per account per region.
exp.d: Incorrect. 1,000,000 is far too high.

q: What is the default maximum number of mount targets per file system?

opts.b: 1 per Availability Zone in the VPC

exp.a: Incorrect. You can have one mount target per AZ, not per VPC.
exp.b: Correct. One mount target per AZ per file system (so up to the number of AZs in the region).
exp.c: Incorrect. There is a limit of one per AZ.
exp.d: Incorrect. It's one per AZ, not a fixed 5 per region.

q: EFS supports which type of read consistency?

opts.d: Consistency only within the same AZ

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS provides strong consistency for certain operations.
exp.b: Correct. EFS provides read-after-write consistency for data-write operations.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS does provide consistency guarantees.
exp.d: Incorrect. Consistency applies across all AZs.

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid use case for Amazon EFS?

exp.a: Incorrect. CMS and web serving are valid EFS use cases.
exp.b: Incorrect. Big data analytics is a valid EFS use case.
exp.c: Correct. EFS cannot be used as a boot volume. EBS is used for boot volumes.
exp.d: Incorrect. Home directories are a common EFS use case.

q: What is Amazon EFS Replication?

opts.a: Replicating data between S3 and EFS
opts.b: Automatically replicating an EFS file system to another AWS Region or AZ
opts.d: Syncing data between EBS and EFS

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS Replication is between EFS file systems, not S3.
exp.b: Correct. EFS Replication automatically replicates data to a destination file system in another region or AZ.
exp.c: Incorrect. Replication is automatic, not manual snapshots.
exp.d: Incorrect. It replicates EFS to EFS, not EBS to EFS.

q: What is the RPO (Recovery Point Objective) for EFS Replication?

exp.a: Incorrect. 24 hours is too long; EFS Replication has a shorter RPO.
exp.b: Correct. EFS Replication is designed to provide an RPO of 15 minutes for most file systems.
exp.c: Incorrect. 1 hour is longer than the typical EFS Replication RPO.
exp.d: Incorrect. While some replications may be faster, the designed RPO is 15 minutes.

q: What helper utility is used to mount EFS on EC2 instances?

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS CLI is a command-line tool but not specifically for mounting EFS.
exp.b: Correct. The amazon-efs-utils package provides the EFS mount helper for simplified mounting.
exp.c: Incorrect. aws-mount-tool is not a real AWS utility.
exp.d: Incorrect. While NFS client can mount EFS, amazon-efs-utils is the recommended helper.

q: Which EFS feature allows you to enforce POSIX user and group for application access?

exp.a: Incorrect. Lifecycle Management moves files between storage classes.
exp.b: Correct. EFS Access Points can enforce POSIX user ID, group ID, and root directory.
exp.c: Incorrect. Replication copies data to another location.
exp.d: Incorrect. Provisioned Throughput sets throughput levels.

q: Can you use Amazon EFS with Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service)?

opts.b: Yes, EFS can be used with ECS tasks (both EC2 and Fargate launch types)

exp.a: Incorrect. ECS supports EFS volumes.
exp.b: Correct. EFS is supported with both EC2 and Fargate launch types in ECS.
exp.c: Incorrect. Both launch types are supported.
exp.d: Incorrect. Both launch types support EFS.

q: What is the Elastic Throughput mode in EFS?

opts.b: A mode that automatically scales throughput up and down based on workload
opts.c: A mode only available for One Zone storage

exp.a: Incorrect. Elastic throughput is not fixed.
exp.b: Correct. Elastic Throughput automatically scales throughput up or down based on workload demands.
exp.c: Incorrect. Elastic Throughput is available for all storage classes.
exp.d: Incorrect. Elastic Throughput is a current and supported mode.

q: What is the maximum throughput achievable with EFS in Elastic Throughput mode for reads?

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS Elastic mode can achieve higher read throughput.
exp.b: Incorrect. 3 GiB/s is the write throughput limit.
exp.c: Correct. EFS Elastic Throughput mode supports up to 10 GiB/s for reads.
exp.d: Incorrect. 5 GiB/s is not the maximum read throughput.

q: What is the maximum write throughput in EFS Elastic Throughput mode?

exp.a: Incorrect. 1 GiB/s is lower than the actual maximum.
exp.b: Correct. EFS Elastic Throughput supports up to 3 GiB/s for writes.
exp.c: Incorrect. 10 GiB/s is the read throughput maximum.
exp.d: Incorrect. 5 GiB/s is not the write throughput maximum.

q: What is the latency characteristic of EFS General Purpose performance mode?

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS General Purpose has low latency.
exp.b: Incorrect. Sub-millisecond is more characteristic of EBS io2.
exp.c: Correct. EFS General Purpose mode provides low, single-digit millisecond latencies.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS latency is in the single-digit milliseconds range.

q: Which EFS performance mode should you choose for highly parallelized workloads like big data and media processing?

exp.a: Incorrect. General Purpose is for latency-sensitive workloads.
exp.b: Correct. Max I/O is designed for highly parallelized applications that need higher aggregate throughput.
exp.c: Incorrect. Bursting is a throughput mode, not a performance mode.
exp.d: Incorrect. Provisioned is a throughput mode.

q: Does Amazon EFS automatically grow and shrink as you add and remove files?

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS is elastic and requires no manual intervention.
exp.b: Correct. EFS automatically grows and shrinks as files are added or removed.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS both grows and shrinks automatically.
exp.d: Incorrect. Auto-scaling applies to all EFS modes.

q: Which service would you use instead of EFS for a high-performance computing (HPC) workload requiring a Lustre file system?

exp.a: Incorrect. EBS is block storage, not a parallel file system.
exp.b: Incorrect. S3 is object storage.
exp.c: Correct. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides a high-performance Lustre file system for HPC.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS Max I/O is not a Lustre file system.

q: What happens if an Availability Zone goes down and you are using EFS Standard storage class?

opts.b: Data remains available from other AZs
opts.c: You need to restore from backup

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS Standard stores data across multiple AZs.
exp.b: Correct. Since EFS Standard stores data across multiple AZs, data remains accessible from other AZs.
exp.c: Incorrect. No restore is needed; data is automatically available.
exp.d: Incorrect. The file system remains fully operational.

q: How is EFS data protected against hardware failures?

opts.b: Data is redundantly stored across multiple AZs (Standard) or within an AZ (One Zone)

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS doesn't use RAID; it uses distributed storage.
exp.b: Correct. EFS automatically stores data redundantly for durability.
exp.c: Incorrect. Protection is built into the service.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS provides high durability through redundant storage.

q: Can you transfer data from on-premises NFS storage to Amazon EFS?

opts.a: No, you must recreate all data manually
opts.c: Only using S3 as an intermediary

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS provides tools for data transfer.
exp.b: Correct. AWS DataSync can transfer data from on-premises NFS/SMB to EFS.
exp.c: Incorrect. DataSync can transfer directly to EFS without S3.
exp.d: Incorrect. Snowball transfers to S3, not directly to EFS.

q: Which AWS service is best suited to transfer large amounts of data to EFS from on-premises?

exp.a: Incorrect. Transfer Family is for SFTP/FTPS/FTP transfers to S3 or EFS but DataSync is optimized for large-scale migration.
exp.b: Correct. AWS DataSync is specifically designed for fast, automated data transfers to EFS.
exp.c: Incorrect. Snowball transfers to S3, not directly to EFS.
exp.d: Incorrect. Storage Gateway is for hybrid cloud storage with S3 backend.

q: What is the durability of Amazon EFS Standard storage class?

exp.a: Incorrect. 99.9% is far lower than EFS durability.
exp.b: Incorrect. 99.99% is the availability SLA, not durability.
exp.c: Correct. EFS Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS provides 11 nines of durability.

q: Which of the following statements about EFS and VPC is correct?

opts.a: EFS file systems can only be accessed from the VPC in which they were created
opts.b: EFS can be accessed from other VPCs using VPC Peering or Transit Gateway
opts.c: EFS does not require a VPC
opts.d: EFS uses public IP addresses for access

exp.a: Incorrect. EFS can be accessed from other VPCs via VPC peering.
exp.b: Correct. EFS can be accessed across VPCs using VPC Peering or AWS Transit Gateway.
exp.c: Incorrect. EFS mount targets are created within VPC subnets.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS uses private IP addresses within the VPC.

q: What is the minimum storage charge for an EFS file system?

opts.b: No minimum; you pay for what you use

exp.a: Incorrect. There is no minimum storage requirement.
exp.b: Correct. EFS has no minimum fee or setup charge; you pay only for storage used.
exp.c: Incorrect. There is no 10 GB minimum.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is no 100 GB minimum.
